name: Q and Not U
label: Dischord
lede: Seven years, three albums, thirty-one kids in primary colors on one album cover, and a D.C. punk band that decided the crowd should dance.

eras.title: A new band from the ashes of a few old ones
eras.text: By the late '90s the D.C. scene that built Dischord had grown up, and Q and Not U were among the first of the next generation to get noticed. They formed out of several broken-up bands and spent their first year in basements and living rooms.

years.p: [[Chris Richards|0065280c-f561-4035-aa65-e9927988d72e]] and [[Harris Klahr|c788433e-623b-4e6c-8998-7c372b8d51b7]] on guitars and vocals, [[John Davis|4729cedd-e42f-4836-8332-6cd316e60268]] on drums and vocals, Matt Borlik on bass.
Dischord dates the band's first live dates to November 1998, a few months after they started practicing.

A string of house shows becomes what the Washington City Paper calls the band's coming-out party. [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] takes notice, drawn to the band's own musical language and the tight crowd forming around it.

eras.title: Thirty-one punks in primary colors
eras.text: Dischord put them out, MacKaye produced them, and the debut album's cover became a group portrait of D.C. punk's next wave. Then came the long tours, and the first member out.

years.p: The first single, a joint release with DeSoto.

years.h: Ten days at Inner Ear with MacKaye
years.p: The band had grown up on Dischord records and asked MacKaye to work with them. He produces the debut at [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]]'s Inner Ear in about ten days.

q: We were just waiting for some custodian to bust us.
years.h: The cover shoot: a borrowed seminar room and 31 kids
years.p: Richards gathers 31 young D.C. punks, mostly under 25, dressed in red, yellow and blue, in a George Washington University art department seminar room. Shawn Brackbill shoots them. The picture turns into a snapshot of a new scene.
years.xp: The shoot wasn't exactly sanctioned. Richards remembered the whole room half expecting to be thrown out.

years.h: No Kill No Beep Beep · Dischord No. 123
years.p: The debut: jagged guitars, three voices trading lines, and a rhythm section built to make people move.

Long tours alongside [[Engine Down|65c54877-7b81-4cb1-8e6b-dc14fbec8b43]], [[Milemarker|151cbcfa-4618-4f26-a769-f15d33743262]], [[Ted Leo and the Pharmacists|31095622-5a1e-4f22-8ad1-b08eb6255f37]] and [[El Guapo|be23bf0a-67c6-4b2f-ba2a-89d983f5ebdd]].

years.h: Borlik out, and nobody replaces him
years.p: After two years of touring, the band dismisses Borlik, as Wikipedia puts it, and carries on as a three-piece. Richards takes over the bass parts.

eras.title: Three people, more sounds
eras.text: Down to a trio, Q and Not U got stranger and bolder rather than smaller. They toured the U.S., Europe, Canada and Japan, and kept Dischord supplied with records.

years.p: The first release as a trio.
The second album, made without a dedicated bass player. Richards covers bass alongside guitar and vocals.
Two songs on a Dischord single (No. 141), a pointer toward the next record.

eras.title: Make them dance, then stop
eras.text: The last album went hard at the one thing D.C. punk shows rarely had: dancing. A year later the band called it off while they were still climbing, with a statement that sounded more like a thank-you than a breakup.

years.big: A D.C. punk band that wanted you dancing.
q: No one ever danced at shows, so we wanted something that got people excited.
years.p: The third and final album, and the one the band built most deliberately for dancing.
years.xp: Davis has said the goal was straightforward: get people moving at shows where nobody moved.

years.p: After seven years, the band says it has reached its shared goals and it's a natural time to stop. They add that they hope to play together again someday.
Nine days after the announcement, the band plays the Siren Music Festival on the Coney Island boardwalk, one of their last shows outside D.C.

years.h: A free show at Fort Reno
years.p: A Monday night gig at D.C.'s free summer concert series in the park, already on the calendar before the breakup news, becomes one of the goodbyes.
A remix EP comes out as the band winds down.

After finishing their touring commitments, Q and Not U close with two nights at the Black Cat on 14th Street, a Thursday and a Friday. Fans who were there told Brooklyn Vegan the last song was Soft Pyramids.
years.xp: The Fort Reno show had been booked well before the July announcement; the Black Cat dates were added afterward as the proper send-off.

eras.title: The critic and the Paint Branch
eras.text: The three went their own ways: Davis into pop with Georgie James and later Title Tracks, Klahr into his own projects in New York, and Richards into solo records as Ris Paul Ric and, eventually, the newspaper. Two of them ended up in a band together again.

years.p: The band's guitarist, bassist and cover-shoot organizer becomes the paper's pop music critic.
The two reunite in a new band, active through 2014 and listed on Dischord's Q and Not U page.

eras.title: The drummer keeps the files
eras.text: The band's drummer became the keeper of the scene's paper trail: archivist at the University of Maryland, where D.C. punk's zines and flyers live, and then its historian.

years.p: The Washington Post profiles Davis keeping D.C. punk alive at a University of Maryland library, where he looks after the scene's collected papers.

Davis publishes a history of D.C. punk fanzines, and launches it at Politics and Prose in conversation with [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]], the man who produced his band's first album.
